set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: What is said about the course of atopic allergies over a lifetime?
opts: Lifelong, outgrown, or appearing later
Correct, and allergy can also be affected by age, infection and geographic area, so the picture is not fixed at any point.
They are always lifelong once established
They may also be outgrown, so the course is not fixed once an allergy is established.
They only ever appear in childhood
They may also develop later in life rather than being confined to childhood onset.
They resolve in every patient by adulthood
They may be lifelong, so resolution by adulthood is not universal.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 8

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: Why do allergic reactions use the same machinery as antiparasitic defence?
opts: Allergens are all derived from parasites
Allergens are described as SIMILAR to parasitic antigens rather than derived from parasites.
The immune system cannot produce IgG against allergens
IgG is produced against allergens, and it is central to how desensitisation works.
Many allergens resemble parasitic antigens
Correct, and the same cells and mechanisms that defend against multicellular parasites are the ones involved in allergic reactions.
Parasites and allergens are both intracellular
The relevant parasites are multicellular and extracellular; the resemblance is antigenic rather than anatomical.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 6

set1.io: 4 — Describe the mechanism of transfusion reactions
set1.q: When does an Rh negative person produce anti-Rh antibodies?
opts: Only if they are also ABO incompatible
Rh sensitisation is independent of ABO grouping and requires prior exposure to Rh positive cells.
Only after sensitisation
Correct — unlike ABO, where antibodies against the antigens you lack are already present, Rh requires prior exposure. A bad transfusion or an incompatible pregnancy does it.
From birth, without any exposure
Rh negative individuals do NOT produce anti-Rh antibodies unless sensitised.
Whenever they encounter any foreign protein
Sensitisation is specific, through bad transfusion or incompatible pregnancy.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 36

set1.io: 1 — Describe the types of immunopathologies
set1.q: Which four categories of immunopathology are described?
opts: Infection, inflammation, necrosis and repair
These are general tissue responses rather than the four categories of immune system malfunction named.
Bacterial, viral, fungal and parasitic disease
These classify pathogens rather than describing ways the immune system itself goes wrong.
Innate, adaptive, humoral and cellular
These are divisions of normal immune function rather than categories of immunopathology.
Allergy, autoimmunity, immunodeficiency and cancer
Correct, and they sort neatly by direction: allergy and autoimmunity are overreactions, while immunodeficiency and cancer are underreactions.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 3

set1.io: 4 — Describe the mechanism of transfusion reactions
set1.q: How is haemolytic disease of the newborn prevented?
opts: Transfusing the mother with Rh positive blood
Transfusing the mother with Rh positive blood would sensitise her rather than protect her.
Cross-matching the fetus against the mother
Cross-matching is a transfusion compatibility test rather than a preventive measure here.
Passive immunisation with anti-Rh antibody
Correct — Rhogam prevents sensitisation of the mother, which is why it must be given before her own response can develop.
Active immunisation of the mother against Rh
The approach is PASSIVE immunisation, giving preformed antibody rather than provoking her own.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 36

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: Which are the general targets of a type I reaction?
opts: Liver and spleen
Neither liver nor spleen is among the general targets named for a type I reaction.
Joints and kidneys
Joint and kidney involvement is typical of immune complex disease, type III.
Skin, airway, gut and conjunctiva
Correct, producing rashes, itching, redness, rhinitis, sneezing, diarrhoea and tears respectively.
Bone marrow and lymph nodes
Those are sites of immune cell production rather than targets of the allergic response.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 12

set1.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
set1.q: Why does it matter to distinguish allergy from infection?
opts: Infection never produces respiratory symptoms
Infection commonly does, which is exactly why the two can be confused.
Allergy testing can also diagnose infection
Allergy tests identify sensitisation to an allergen rather than detecting infection.
They present similarly but differ entirely
Correct, and this is why diagnosis uses objective methods — skin testing, blood tests and supervised challenge — rather than symptoms alone.
Allergy is always more severe than infection
Severity varies in both; the distinction is about the underlying process.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 25

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: Which autoimmune disorders are named as type III?
opts: Multiple sclerosis and type 1 diabetes
Those involve T cell mediated destruction rather than immune complexes.
Graves disease and Hashimoto thyroiditis
Those are endocrine autoimmunities involving autoantibodies against thyroid targets.
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and lupus
Correct, and all three fit the pattern: immune complexes depositing in joints, skin and kidney, the tissues typical of complex disease. Rheumatoid arthritis too.
Myasthenia gravis and autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
Those are type II, where antibody binds cell surface antigens.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 39

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: What causes serum sickness?
opts: A second vaccine injection at the same site
That describes the Arthus reaction, a localised dermal injury from inflamed blood vessels.
Inhalation of a protein allergen
Inhaled protein allergens produce type I rhinitis and asthma rather than serum sickness.
Contact with metals or cosmetics
Contact with metals or cosmetics produces contact dermatitis, a type IV reaction.
Exposure to foreign animal proteins
Correct — horse serum used in tetanus treatment is the example, along with animal hormones or drugs. Complexes lodge in heart, kidneys, skin and joints.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 39

set1.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
set1.q: What is a physician-supervised challenge used for?
opts: Confirming transfusion compatibility
Confirming transfusion compatibility is the role of cross-matching rather than of a challenge.
Food allergies when other tests are inconclusive
Correct — it is the fallback when skin and blood testing leave the question open, and supervision is required because the response can be severe.
Screening every patient for inhaled allergens
It is reserved for inconclusive food allergy questions rather than used as a screen.
Diagnosing contact dermatitis
Patch testing is what is typically used for contact dermatitis.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 25

set1.io: 4 — Describe the mechanism of transfusion reactions
set1.q: What does the cross-match test compare?
opts: Recipient serum against donor serum
The test sets serum against cells rather than serum against serum.
Donor red cells against recipient red cells
One side of the test must supply antibody, which means serum.
Recipient serum against donor red cells
Correct, and the reverse is not performed: even with whole blood there is not enough antibody in donor serum to reach the density on red cells needed for a reaction.
Donor serum against recipient red cells
That direction is specifically NOT tested, because the antibody quantity is insufficient.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 34

set1.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
set1.q: What does prevention of allergy involve?
opts: Administering epinephrine prophylactically
Epinephrine is used to reverse an acute reaction rather than to prevent exposure.
Modifying environment and behaviour
Correct, and it is listed first because removing the trigger is the only approach that does not depend on blunting a normal mechanism. The aim is to avoid the allergen entirely.
Taking antihistamines daily regardless of exposure
Taking antihistamines regardless of exposure is pharmacological control rather than prevention.
Injecting small amounts of the allergen
Injecting small amounts of allergen is desensitisation, the third of the three approaches.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 27

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: What is familial about allergy?
opts: A generalised predisposition
Correct — families inherit the tendency rather than the particular allergen, which is why relatives may react to entirely different things. The specific allergy is not inherited.
The specific allergen a person reacts to
The inherited element is the general predisposition rather than the specific allergy.
The route by which allergens enter
Portal of entry is determined by exposure rather than inherited.
Nothing — allergy has no familial component
A generalised predisposition to allergies is specifically described as familial.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 8

set1.io: 4 — Describe the mechanism of transfusion reactions
set1.q: Why must ABO antigens be matched in transfusion?
opts: Transfused cells are permanent replacements
Transfusions are described as temporary rather than as permanent cell replacements.
There are no MHC molecules on red blood cells
Correct, so ABO is the critical matching system. You carry antibodies in your serum against the antigens you lack, and mismatch can be fatal through complement activation and lysis.
MHC matching is more important than ABO for red cells
Red blood cells carry NO MHC molecules, which is what makes ABO critical.
Red cells carry the full set of HLA antigens
They do not; the absence of MHC on red cells is the stated reason ABO matters.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 33

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: Why does helminth infection not produce allergic disease despite raising IgE?
opts: Eosinophil numbers fall during infection
Eosinophils and mast cells INCREASE in helminth infection, which is why the absence of allergy needs explaining.
Nonspecific IgE competes for Fc receptors
Correct, crowding out parasite-specific and allergen-specific IgE. T cell responses are also suppressed in chronic parasitic infection by regulatory T cells.
Helminths destroy mast cells directly
The mechanism described is competition for receptor binding rather than destruction of the cells.
IgE is not involved in allergic disease
IgE is responsible for most allergic responses; the point is which IgE occupies the receptors.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 7

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: What is required for a type III reaction to occur?
opts: Prior sensitisation with IgE
IgE sensitisation is the type I mechanism, in which cell-bound antibody is crosslinked by allergen.
A T cell mediated memory response
T cell memory drives type IV rather than immune complex disease.
Only a trace of antigen
A LARGE amount of antigen is specified, which is why serum sickness follows bulk protein exposure.
A large amount of antigen
Correct, which is part of why serum sickness follows exposure to foreign animal proteins in quantity rather than to a trace allergen.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 38

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: What is the chain of events leading to death in systemic anaphylaxis?
opts: Fluid leaves the blood and pressure drops
Correct, ending in organ damage and asphyxiation from the constricted airways. It causes 500 to 1,000 deaths a year in the United States. Tissue swells and the airways constrict.
Red cells lyse and block the glomeruli
Red cell lysis blocking the glomeruli is the transfusion reaction pathway, a type II event.
Immune complexes accumulate in the heart and kidneys
Complexes accumulating in heart and kidneys describes serum sickness, a type III reaction.
T cells gradually destroy the airway epithelium
Gradual T cell destruction of epithelium is the slow cellular mechanism of type IV.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 22

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: What do eosinophils release in an IgE response?
opts: Complement components
Complement is produced largely by the liver rather than released by eosinophils.
Toxic mediators
Correct, and their defensive role explains the allergic one: they are used against EUKARYOTIC PARASITES, and allergens resemble parasitic antigens.
Histamine from preformed granules only
Histamine release is the mast cell's characteristic contribution; eosinophils release toxic mediators.
Antibodies of the IgE class
Antibody is produced by B cells; eosinophils are granulocyte effectors.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 5

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: How many IgE molecules can each mast cell bind?
opts: Between 10,000 and 40,000
Correct, which explains the scale of the response — a single cell carries an enormous number of trigger points for crosslinking.
Between 10 and 40
The figure is three orders of magnitude larger, at 10,000 to 40,000.
Exactly one
Crosslinking requires many bound antibodies, and each cell binds tens of thousands.
Between 100 and 400
The number given is 10,000 to 40,000 IgE molecules per cell, not hundreds.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 12

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: What does the late phase reaction achieve?
opts: It attracts more cells and sensitises the tissue
Correct — eosinophils are drawn in, their cytokines enhance inflammation, and the tissue becomes more sensitive to subsequent allergic reactions.
It terminates the allergic response
It extends and amplifies the response rather than ending it.
It produces immediate mast cell degranulation
Degranulation is the immediate reaction; the late phase is driven by synthesised mediators.
It clears immune complexes from the tissue
Immune complexes belong to type III rather than to the IgE late phase.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 23

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: What are the systemic targets of a type I reaction?
opts: Smooth muscle, mucous glands, nerve
Correct, and the responses are vascular dilation and constriction, producing changes in blood pressure and respiration.
Skin, conjunctiva and nasal mucosa
Those are among the GENERAL targets rather than the systemic ones.
Red blood cells and platelets
Those are targets in type II reactions such as transfusion incompatibility.
Basement membranes of epithelial tissue
Basement membranes of epithelial tissue are where type III immune complexes deposit instead.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 12

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: Which allergens and routes are named for anaphylaxis?
opts: Inhaled pollens only
Inhaled allergens cause rhinitis and asthma; the anaphylaxis routes named are injection and oral.
Contact with metals and cosmetics
Contact with metals and cosmetics produces contact dermatitis, a delayed type IV reaction.
Transfused red blood cells
Transfused red cells provoke a type II reaction against cell surface antigens rather than anaphylaxis.
Bee stings and antibiotics by injection
Correct, and the variability of both allergen and route is the point — what matters is that the allergen reaches the bloodstream. Serum too, and peanuts by the oral route.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 21

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: What antibody class mediates type I hypersensitivity?
opts: IgG and IgM binding cell surface antigens
That describes type II, where free antibody binds to cell surface antigens and activates complement.
IgG and IgM binding soluble antigens
That describes type III, where immune complexes form and embed in basement membranes.
No antibody — it is T cell mediated
That describes type IV, the delayed hypersensitivity reaction.
IgE
Correct, and the reaction is IMMEDIATE — cell-bound antibody is crosslinked and inflammatory mediators are released from mast cells, basophils and eosinophils.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 9

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: What happens in the nose during allergic rhinitis?
opts: Histamine raises capillary permeability
Correct, and eosinophils are then attracted from the blood, release inflammatory mediators, and are shed into the nasal passage. The nasal epithelium is activated to make mucus.
Immune complexes deposit in the nasal basement membrane
Complex deposition is the type III mechanism rather than the rhinitis pathway.
Cytotoxic T cells destroy nasal epithelium
Cytotoxic T cell destruction of epithelium characterises type IV rather than allergic rhinitis.
Complement lyses the nasal mucosal cells
Complement activation belongs to types II and III rather than to the rhinitis pathway.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 17

set1.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
set1.q: What is the most common form of allergen specific immunotherapy?
opts: Inhaled allergen challenge
Inhaled challenge is not among the described desensitisation routes.
Subcutaneous immunotherapy
Correct — small amounts of allergen introduced by injection, improving reactions in about 80 per cent of those who complete the process.
Sublingual immunotherapy
Sublingual immunotherapy is used more in other parts of the world than in the United States.
Intravenous allergen infusion
The named routes are subcutaneous injection and sublingual administration.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 29

set1.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
set1.q: What has a four-year trial shown about sublingual immunotherapy for peanut allergy?
opts: It works only for peanut and no other food
It has also been shown effective against kiwi, hazelnut, milk and peach.
It is effective and safe

Correct, and it appears to provide safety against accidental exposures. It has also been shown effective against kiwi, hazelnut, milk and peach allergies. The dose is about one seventy-fifth of a kernel.
It cures peanut allergy permanently in all patients
The described benefit is protection against accidental exposure rather than a permanent cure in everyone.
It requires a whole peanut kernel per dose
The quantity is a tiny fraction — about one seventy-fifth of a kernel.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 31

set1.io: 4 — Describe the mechanism of transfusion reactions
set1.q: When is Rhogam administered?
opts: Only at the time of delivery
It is also given antenatally at 26 to 28 weeks rather than only at the time of delivery.
Only before the first pregnancy
It is given during and after each at-risk pregnancy rather than once.
Only if the first child was affected
The point is to prevent sensitisation before any child is affected.
At 26 to 28 weeks, and after birth
Correct, and also after prenatal invasive tests, abdominal injury or accidental exposure — any event that could mix fetal and maternal blood. The postnatal dose is within 72 hours.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 37

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: What mediates type IV hypersensitivity?
opts: IgE bound to mast cells
IgE bound to mast cells drives type I, the immediate reaction rather than the delayed one.
IgG and IgM with complement
IgG and IgM drive types II and III, binding cell surface antigens and soluble antigens respectively.
Complement alone, without cells
Complement participates in types II and III; type IV is cell mediated.
T cells
Correct — cytotoxic cells destroy tissue, and because the response requires cellular recruitment rather than preformed antibody, it is DELAYED.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 9

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: When does the late phase reaction occur?
opts: About six hours afterwards
Correct, mediated by synthesised products such as leukotrienes rather than by preformed granule contents.
Within the first minute
The immediate reaction is the wheal and flare from mast cell degranulation; the late phase follows about six hours later.
After several weeks
The interval given is roughly six hours rather than a matter of weeks.
Only after a second sensitising dose
It follows the same exposure, as the second half of one IgE-mediated reaction.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 23

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: Which are named as infectious allergy examples of type IV?
opts: Transfusion reactions and haemolytic disease of the newborn
Those are type II, involving antibody against cell surface antigens.
Serum sickness and the Arthus reaction
Serum sickness and the Arthus reaction are type III, mediated by immune complexes.
Tuberculosis, leprosy, syphilis and histoplasmosis
Correct, with toxoplasmosis and candidiasis completing the list — chronic infections where the T cell response itself damages tissue.
Hay fever and anaphylaxis
Hay fever and anaphylaxis are type I, IgE mediated and immediate rather than delayed and cellular.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 40

set2.io: 1 — Describe the types of immunopathologies
set2.q: How is allergy or hypersensitivity defined?
opts: A loss or deficiency of immune function
That is immunodeficiency, an underreaction rather than an overreaction.
An exaggerated, misdirected immune response to an allergen
Correct, and the critical point is that it uses the SAME mechanisms as protective immune reactions — nothing novel is happening, it is simply happening against the wrong target.
A response using mechanisms unique to allergic disease
The mechanisms are the same as those used in protective immunity; only the target and the magnitude differ.
An abnormal response directed against self antigens
That is autoimmunity, which is directed at self rather than at an external allergen.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 3

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: Which tissues are typically involved in immune complex disease?
opts: Joint, skin and kidney
Correct, and the symptoms are DELAYED by hours to days, unlike the immediate reaction of type I.
Lung and liver exclusively
The typical triad named is joint, skin and kidney rather than lung and liver.
Bone marrow and thymus
Those are sites of immune cell development rather than typical immune complex deposition.
Brain and spinal cord
The central nervous system is named among immunologically privileged sites rather than as typical for complex deposition.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 38

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: Why does a food allergen produce urticaria in the skin?
opts: Skin mast cells are sensitised by ingestion directly
The antigen reaches the skin through the bloodstream rather than sensitising skin cells directly.
Immune complexes deposit in dermal vessels
That is a type III mechanism rather than the described food allergy route.
Antigen enters blood vessels and is carried to the skin
Correct, which is the clearest illustration that the organ of allergic expression need not be the portal of entry.
Mast cells migrate from the gut to the skin
The antigen travels through the bloodstream rather than the mast cells migrating to the skin.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 18

set2.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
set2.q: What are the three general methods of managing type I hypersensitivity?
opts: Prevention, pharmacology, desensitisation
Correct, and they escalate: avoid the allergen, blunt the response, or retrain the immune system against it.
Antibiotics, antivirals and antifungals
Antibiotics, antivirals and antifungals treat infection rather than managing hypersensitivity.
Surgery, radiation and chemotherapy
Surgery, radiation and chemotherapy are cancer treatments rather than allergy management methods.
Transfusion, transplantation and grafting
Those relate to types II and IV rather than to allergy management.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 26

set2.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
set2.q: Which skin tests are used in allergy diagnosis?
opts: Cross-matching against donor red cells
Cross-matching recipient serum against donor red cells is a transfusion compatibility test.
Skin prick testing and intradermal testing
Correct, both producing wheal and flare reactions. The patch test is separate and is used for contact dermatitis, a type IV reaction.
Patch testing alone
Patch testing is typically used for CONTACT DERMATITIS rather than for type I allergy.
Tuberculin testing
The tuberculin skin test assesses a type IV response to mycobacterial antigen.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 25

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: What happens on the sensitising dose in type I allergy?
opts: T cells are recruited to the site of contact
T cell recruitment to the site characterises type IV, the delayed hypersensitivity reaction.
B cells form IgE, which arms mast cells
Correct, and generally there are no signs or symptoms at this stage — the patient is being armed without knowing it. Basophils are armed the same way.
Mast cells degranulate and symptoms appear
Degranulation occurs on the PROVOCATIVE dose, at subsequent exposure.
Immune complexes form and deposit in tissue
Immune complex formation and deposition is the type III mechanism rather than the sensitising dose.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 12

set2.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
set2.q: Which blood findings support an allergy diagnosis?
opts: Specific IgE and increased basophils
Correct, and they complement the skin tests by measuring the sensitisation directly rather than through a provoked skin reaction.
Raised IgG against the allergen
Allergen-specific IgG is what desensitisation therapy aims to RAISE, blocking the allergen from IgE.
Complement consumption
Complement activation features in types II and III rather than in type I diagnosis.
Positive blood culture
A positive blood culture would indicate infection rather than supporting an allergy diagnosis.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 25

set2.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
set2.q: What does cromolyn sodium do?
opts: Reverses airway constriction directly
That is epinephrine, which also re-establishes endothelial tight junctions.
Blocks degranulation
Correct — it prevents the mast cell from releasing its granule contents rather than blocking the mediators afterwards.
Reduces IgE production by inhibiting lymphocytes
Reducing IgE production by inhibiting lymphocytes is the corticosteroid mechanism.
Binds to IgE as a monoclonal antibody
Binding IgE as a monoclonal antibody describes omalizumab rather than cromolyn sodium.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 28

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: What do basophils initiate?
opts: A TH1 response and production of IgG
The response they initiate is TH2 with IgE, which is the allergic axis.
Complement activation by the classical pathway
Complement activation characterises types II and III rather than the basophil's initiating role.
Cytotoxic T cell proliferation
Cytotoxic T cells belong to type IV responses rather than to the basophil-driven IgE axis.
A TH2 response and production of IgE
Correct. They are rare granulocytes, and in normal defence they act against helminths — the same axis that produces allergy when misdirected.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 5

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: Which skin responses fall under type IV?
opts: The tuberculin skin test
Correct, with contact dermatitis arising from plants, metals and cosmetics. Graft rejection is the third category of type IV T cell response. Contact dermatitis too.
Wheal and flare reactions
Wheal and flare is the IMMEDIATE type I reaction, used in allergy skin testing.
Urticaria from ingested food
Urticaria follows histamine release from skin mast cells in a type I reaction rather than a delayed one.
Angioedema
Angioedema results from mast cell activation deeper in the skin, a type I mechanism.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 40

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: What immune response does helminth infection stimulate?
opts: Complement-mediated lysis of the parasite
The described response is TH2, IgE, eosinophils and mast cells.
No adaptive response at all
A strong adaptive TH2 response is precisely what is stimulated.
CD4 TH2-like responses with high IgE
Correct, together with an increase in eosinophils and mast cells — exactly the profile of allergic disease, which is why the absence of allergy needs explaining.
CD8 cytotoxic responses with high IgG
The response described is TH2 with IgE rather than a cytotoxic IgG response.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 7

set2.io: 1 — Describe the types of immunopathologies
set2.q: Which hypersensitivity types are B cell mediated?
opts: Types I and II only
Type III is also antibody driven, through immune complexes of IgG and IgM.
Type IV only
Type IV is the T CELL mediated one, standing apart from the other three.
All four types
Type IV is T cell mediated rather than B cell mediated, which is what sets it apart.
Types I, II and III
Correct, and type IV is the exception — it is T cell mediated, which is why it is delayed rather than immediate.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 3

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: How many people are heavily and persistently infected with helminths?
opts: About one billion
Correct, in countries where helminth infection is endemic — and notably those populations do not show corresponding allergic disease.
About one million
The figure given is a thousand times larger, at around one billion.
About ten thousand
The burden described is of the order of one billion people heavily and persistently infected.
Fewer than one hundred thousand
Helminth infection is endemic across tropical countries, affecting around one billion heavily.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 7

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: What distinguishes angioedema from urticaria?
opts: A different antibody class is involved
Both urticaria and angioedema are IgE-driven mast cell events; only the depth differs.
It is T cell rather than antibody mediated
T cell mediation describes type IV reactions such as contact dermatitis.
It is a more prolonged response
The more prolonged allergic response in the skin is atopic dermatitis, or eczema.
Mast cell activation deeper in the skin
Correct. The mechanism is identical; the depth at which it happens is what changes the appearance.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 16

set2.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
set2.q: How do injected allergens block the allergic response?
opts: They destroy circulating IgE directly
Direct action against IgE describes omalizumab rather than immunotherapy.
They induce tolerance by deleting all B cells
B cells are not deleted; blocking antibody and regulatory T cells are induced.
They raise allergen-specific IgG
Correct, so the mast cells do not degranulate — the allergen is intercepted before it can crosslink the cell-bound antibody. It blocks the allergen from reaching IgE.
They deplete mast cells from the tissue
The mechanism is competitive blocking by IgG rather than removal of the cells.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 29

set2.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
set2.q: How do corticosteroids act in allergy?
opts: They block mast cell degranulation
Blocking mast cell degranulation is what cromolyn sodium does rather than a corticosteroid.
They bind histamine receptors on target organs
Binding histamine receptors on target organs is the antihistamine mechanism.
They block leukotriene synthesis
Blocking leukotriene synthesis is montelukast sodium rather than a corticosteroid.
They inhibit lymphocytes to reduce IgE
Correct, acting upstream on the production of the antibody rather than on the mediators it releases.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 28

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: What do the antibodies bind in type II hypersensitivity?
opts: Nothing — no antibody is involved
Type II is initiated by IgG and IgM; it is type IV that involves no antibody.
Cell surface antigens
Correct, and the consequence follows: complement is activated, with cell lysis by the membrane attack complex and phagocytosis.
Soluble antigens, forming complexes
Binding soluble antigen to form immune complexes is type III.
Antigen already bound to mast cells
Crosslinking of cell-bound IgE on mast cells is type I, the immediate hypersensitivity reaction.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 9

set2.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
set2.q: How does epinephrine act in anaphylaxis?
opts: It reforms tight junctions and relaxes bronchi
Correct, and it also prevents upper airway mucosal oedema, stimulates the heart, and binds receptors on immune cells to suppress histamine release.
It blocks histamine receptors on target organs
That is the antihistamine mechanism rather than epinephrine's.
It blocks synthesis of leukotrienes
Blocking leukotriene synthesis is what montelukast sodium does rather than epinephrine.
It is a monoclonal antibody against IgE
A monoclonal antibody directed against IgE is omalizumab rather than epinephrine.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 22

set2.io: 4 — Describe the mechanism of transfusion reactions
set2.q: Which conditions are given as type II examples?
opts: Hay fever and anaphylaxis
Hay fever and anaphylaxis are type I, mediated by IgE bound to mast cells.
Transfusion reactions and Rh incompatibility
Correct, together with some autoimmune conditions — autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and myasthenia gravis, where antibodies target acetylcholine receptors. ABO incompatibility too.
Serum sickness and the Arthus reaction
Serum sickness and the Arthus reaction are type III, immune complex mediated.
Contact dermatitis and graft rejection
Contact dermatitis and graft rejection are type IV, T cell mediated and delayed.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 32

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: What happens to the immune complexes in type III hypersensitivity?
opts: They bind directly to mast cell IgE
That describes type I, where allergen crosslinks cell-bound IgE.
They are destroyed by cytotoxic T cells
Cytotoxic T cell destruction of tissue characterises type IV.
They embed in basement membranes
Correct, and once trapped they incite a damaging inflammatory response through phagocytosis and complement activation.
They are cleared without consequence
Their deposition is precisely what initiates the inflammatory condition.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 9

set2.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
set2.q: What does FEV1 measure?
opts: The diameter of a wheal on skin testing
Wheal diameter belongs to skin prick testing rather than to a measure of breathing capacity.
Air forcibly exhaled in one second
Correct — the maximum volume, used to plot the immediate response at under an hour against the late phase response after six hours.
Total lung capacity at full inspiration
FEV1 measures forced expiration in one second rather than total capacity.
The concentration of IgE in serum
That is a blood test for specific IgE rather than a breathing measurement.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 24

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: What does the hygiene hypothesis propose?
opts: Exposure to allergens in childhood causes lifelong allergy
The hypothesis runs the opposite way, attributing allergy to too LITTLE early immune challenge.
Hygiene practices directly damage epithelial barriers
The proposed mechanism concerns regulation of the immune system rather than barrier damage.
Vaccination produces IgE against vaccine components
Vaccination is named among the things that reduced parasitic infection rather than as a source of IgE.
Underused immune systems are less successfully regulated
Correct. Better hygiene, vaccination and antibiotics eradicated helminth and other parasitic infections in Western Europe and North America, leaving the system without its usual training.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 7

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: Which are examples of type I hypersensitivity?
opts: Transfusion reactions
Transfusion reactions are the classic type II example, involving cell lysis.
Serum sickness and lupus
Serum sickness and lupus are type III, driven by immune complexes depositing in basement membranes.
Contact dermatitis
Contact dermatitis is type IV, T cell mediated and delayed rather than antibody mediated and immediate.
Hay fever and hives
Correct, and they range from trivial to fatal while sharing one mechanism: IgE crosslinking on mast cells releasing inflammatory mediators. Anaphylactic shock too.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 9

set2.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
set2.q: What is omalizumab?
opts: A leukotriene synthesis blocker
Blocking leukotriene synthesis is montelukast sodium rather than an anti-IgE antibody.
A histamine receptor blocker
Blocking histamine receptors on target organs describes the antihistamines.
A mast cell stabiliser
Blocking degranulation is what cromolyn sodium does rather than an antibody against IgE.
A monoclonal antibody against IgE
Correct, so it removes the antibody that arms the mast cell rather than acting on the cell or its mediators.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 28

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: What is the Arthus reaction?
opts: A delayed T cell response to an injected antigen
The Arthus reaction is immune complex mediated, type III, rather than T cell mediated.
An immediate wheal and flare
An immediate wheal and flare is the type I reaction from mast cell degranulation.
Localised dermal injury from inflamed blood vessels
Correct — a vasculitis, typically following a second injection of vaccine at a site, and normally self limiting.
A systemic reaction to foreign animal protein
That is serum sickness, which deposits complexes in heart, kidneys, skin and joints.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 39

set2.io: 4 — Describe the mechanism of transfusion reactions
set2.q: Which combination produces haemolytic disease of the newborn?
opts: Two Rh negative parents
The fetus must be Rh positive for the mother to be sensitised.
Any ABO mismatch between mother and fetus
The disease described here arises from Rh rather than ABO incompatibility.
An Rh negative mother with an Rh positive fetus
Correct, and the first pregnancy is normally fine because it is the sensitising event; subsequent pregnancies carry the haemolytic risk.
An Rh positive mother with an Rh negative fetus
The mother must lack the antigen in order to be sensitised against it.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 36

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: What is said about the relationship between the portal of entry and the organ affected?
opts: They may or may not be the same
Correct, which is why an ingested food allergen can produce urticaria in the skin — antigen entering blood vessels is carried there.
They are always the same
The organ of allergic expression may differ from the portal of entry.
They are never the same
They may be the same; the point is that this is not guaranteed.
The portal determines the severity but not the site
The statement concerns whether the site matches the portal rather than severity.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 10

set2.io: 4 — Describe the mechanism of transfusion reactions
set2.q: What are the consequences of a transfusion reaction?
opts: Delayed T cell infiltration of the transfused tissue
That would be a type IV mechanism; transfusion reactions are type II.
Bronchial smooth muscle contraction
Bronchial smooth muscle contraction is the acute asthmatic response in type I allergy.
Red cell destruction, glomerular blockage, fever and jaundice
Correct, and even where complement activation is incomplete, antibody-coated cells may attract natural killer cells or macrophages.
Immune complex deposition in joints and skin
Immune complex deposition in joints and skin belongs to type III rather than to transfusion.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 35

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: What characterises systemic anaphylaxis?
opts: Immune complex deposition in joints and kidneys
Complex deposition in joints and kidneys belongs to type III immune complex disease.
Sudden respiratory and circulatory disruption
Correct. Allergen reaches the bloodstream and activates connective tissue mast cells associated with blood vessels throughout the body. It can be fatal in a few minutes.
A localised wheal and flare skin reaction
That is cutaneous anaphylaxis, which is used in the diagnosis of allergies.
A delayed reaction appearing after several days
Anaphylaxis is immediate and can be fatal within minutes rather than appearing after days.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 21

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: What produces urticaria?
opts: Mast cells in the skin releasing histamine
Correct, causing raised itchy swelling. Angioedema is the same process happening in DEEPER skin, and eczema is a more prolonged allergic response.
Immune complexes depositing in dermal vessels
Immune complexes in dermal vessels describe the Arthus reaction, a localised type III event.
Cytotoxic T cells attacking keratinocytes
Cytotoxic T cells attacking keratinocytes belongs to contact dermatitis, a type IV reaction.
Complement lysing skin cells
Complement-mediated lysis characterises type II reactions such as transfusion incompatibility.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 16
